title: What is the actual claim?
prompt: Read the paragraph. Write its main claim and its main reason in ONE sentence: "<claim> because <reason>." 30 words max.
source: Look, everyone keeps talking about microservices, and sure, they're trendy. But our team is six people. Every new service is another thing to deploy, monitor and wake up for at night. Last quarter we spent more time on pipeline glue than on features. I'm not saying never, but right now a modular monolith would let us ship faster.
intent: Claim: the team should use a modular monolith (not microservices) for now. Reason: with only six people, each extra service adds deploy/monitoring/on-call overhead that slowed feature work last quarter.
hints: Skip the opinions about trends. What does the writer want the team to DO?
exampleGood: Our six-person team should build a modular monolith for now because each extra service adds deploy and on-call work that already slowed features.

title: Four-day week
prompt: This argument jumps from evidence to a conclusion. List the unstated assumptions it needs to be true. One per line.
spec: A company in Iceland moved to a four-day work week and its productivity rose 20%. Therefore, if we switch to a four-day week, our productivity will also rise about 20%.

hiddenCases.title: Same kind of company
hiddenCases.description: Assumes our company (industry, type of work, size) is similar enough to the Iceland company for the result to carry over.

hiddenCases.title: The four-day week caused it
hiddenCases.description: Assumes the four-day week caused the rise, not something else that changed at the same time (new tools, economy, hiring).

hiddenCases.title: Productivity measured the same way
hiddenCases.description: Assumes 'productivity' means the same thing and is measured the same way at both companies (output per hour vs per week, etc.).

hiddenCases.title: One case generalizes
hiddenCases.description: Assumes a single company's result is reliable and not a fluke or a cherry-picked example.

hiddenCases.title: Effect lasts
hiddenCases.description: Assumes the gain persists over time and is not a short-term novelty effect.

hiddenCases.title: Context transfers
hiddenCases.description: Assumes national context (culture, labor law, workforce) does not matter.

hints: Ask: what if our company is nothing like that one?
Ask: did anything else change at the same time?

title: Steelman the other side
prompt: You think code review should be required for every change. Write the STRONGEST honest argument against that, in 2 sentences. A fan of the other side should nod.
intent: A strong, fair argument against mandatory review of every change, e.g.: mandatory review on every change adds waiting time and context switching that slows delivery, and for small, low-risk or easily reversible changes with good tests and fast rollback, the cost of the delay can exceed the bugs it catches. Must not be a strawman (e.g. 'reviews are useless' or 'people are lazy').
hints: What does a mandatory review cost, every single time?
For which changes is that cost bigger than the benefit?
exampleGood: Mandatory review makes every change wait for another person, which slows delivery and breaks focus. For small, well-tested changes that are easy to roll back, that delay costs more than the few bugs review would catch.

title: The 5-star app
prompt: List what this conclusion quietly assumes. One per line.
spec: Our app has a 4.9-star average rating in the app store, so our users love the app and we don't need to change anything.

hiddenCases.title: Reviewers represent users
hiddenCases.description: Assumes the people who leave reviews are representative of all users (unhappy users may just leave silently).

hiddenCases.title: Leavers are counted
hiddenCases.description: Assumes people who uninstalled or churned are reflected in the rating (they often are not).

hiddenCases.title: Ratings are not engineered
hiddenCases.description: Assumes the rating is not inflated by when/how the app asks for reviews (e.g. only prompting after a success moment) or by fake/incentivized reviews.

hiddenCases.title: High rating = love
hiddenCases.description: Assumes a high star rating means users love it, rather than finding it acceptable or rating it once long ago.

hiddenCases.title: Good now = no change needed
hiddenCases.description: Assumes that being liked today means nothing needs to change (competitors, growth, new needs, technical debt).

hints: Who does NOT leave a review?
Does liking it today mean it will win tomorrow?
